muga-silk.origin: Muga silk is produced by Antheraea assamensis Helfer, a saturniid silkmoth endemic to northeastern India, with production centered in Assam. Larvae are reared outdoors on trees, principally som (Persea bombycina), and the culture supports rural and tribal households. Researchers at the Central Silk Board's Central Muga Eri Research and Training Institute in Jorhat have reported that air pollution, including emissions near an oil refinery, stresses som trees and is a concern for sustaining production, and A. assamensis is also vulnerable to bacterial and viral diseases that reduce silk yields.
muga-silk.structure: Muga filaments consist of fibroin in a sericin coating, with the flatter, coarser cross-section typical of Antheraea silks. Its fibroin has alanine-rich crystalline domains and contains RGD tripeptide motifs, and comparative testing (Fang et al., 2016) found muga more extensible and tougher in some respects than Bombyx mori silk, with properties tied to beta-sheet content, crystallinity and orientation. The golden color is natural rather than dyed. Muga fibroin has been processed into cryogels and porous scaffolds for liver and cartilage tissue engineering research, where its scaffolds supported more cartilage matrix production than mulberry fibroin in one comparison.
muga-silk.process: Rearing is outdoors on som trees, where larvae must be protected from birds, insects, weather and disease, and they are moved to fresh trees as foliage is consumed. Mature larvae spin cocoons that are stifled and then cooked in mild alkaline solutions before reeling, and the raw silk is traditionally woven on handlooms into Assamese garments such as the mekhela chador, usually in its natural color. Pierced cocoons and waste are spun into lower-grade yarn. Because all stages depend on a single regional host system, weather and pollution directly affect supply.
muga-silk.performance: Muga is valued for durability and its golden luster, which is used in its natural color rather than dyed over. Like other non-mulberry silks it shows higher extensibility than mulberry silk in laboratory tests. As a protein fiber it absorbs moisture, chars rather than melts, and is weakened by alkali, chlorine bleach and prolonged sunlight. Statements that its luster increases with every wash are traditional descriptions rather than standardized test results, and care instructions from the maker should govern cleaning.
muga-silk.identify: Burn tests (indicative only; conduct safely) confirm silk but not species. Microscopy shows the flattened cross-section typical of Antheraea silk, and spectroscopic methods reflect alanine-rich fibroin, but separating muga from other golden wild silks or from dyed mulberry silk can require specialist analysis. Imitation of muga by cheaper silks is a known concern, so buyers should look for registered geographical indication users or Silk Mark labeling and request laboratory testing for high-value pieces.
muga-silk.labeling: The generic fiber name is silk in the US and the EU; muga is a qualifier indicating species and regional origin. In India, Muga Silk of Assam is registered as a geographical indication under the Geographical Indications of Goods (Registration and Protection) Act, 1999, which reserves the registered name for authorized producers of goods from the defined area. A geographical indication protects a name where it is registered but does not itself test fiber purity, so Silk Mark labeling and laboratory testing are complementary tools. Protection outside India depends on local law.
muga-silk.past: Muga has long been part of Assamese textile heritage, and its survival depends on an outdoor rearing system confined to one region. That dependence has shaped recent research: studies on air pollution tolerance of som trees near industrial sites, validation of reference genes for studying A. assamensis immunity under bacterial and viral infection (2025), and a 2025 genome-wide comparison of antimicrobial attacin genes across A. assamensis, A. pernyi, A. mylitta, A. yamamai and Samia ricini. Biomaterials work since the 2010s has added a new, non-textile interest in muga fibroin.

acetate.origin: Acetate starts from purified cellulose, historically cotton linter and more commonly dissolving wood pulp, which is esterified with acetic anhydride in the presence of acetic acid and an acid catalyst. The product is not regenerated cellulose: the acetyl groups stay on the polymer, so the fiber is a cellulose ester. The same cellulose diacetate chemistry also supplies cigarette filter tow and films, so textile filament is only one outlet for a shared intermediate.
acetate.structure: The key variable is the degree of substitution (DS), the average number of the three hydroxyl groups on each anhydroglucose unit that carry an acetyl group. Textile diacetate typically sits around DS 2.4, within a working range of roughly 2 to 2.7, whereas commercial triacetate is about 2.9. Replacing hydroxyls with bulkier, less polar acetyl groups disrupts the hydrogen bonding that makes cotton and viscose absorbent and highly crystalline, so the fiber is more thermoplastic and less water-loving than regenerated cellulose. Filaments usually have a lobed or irregular cross-section with a few longitudinal striations, which helps give the characteristic luster.
acetate.process: Cellulose is fully acetylated first, because acetylation to an exact intermediate level is hard to control directly. The primary triacetate is then partly hydrolyzed (ripened) back to the target DS, precipitated as flake, washed and dried. The flake is dissolved in acetone to make a viscous dope, filtered and pushed through spinnerets into a column of warm air, where the acetone evaporates and the filaments solidify. This dry spinning route allows the solvent to be recovered from the air stream. Filament yarn is then wound, and may be twisted, textured or cut to staple for blending.
acetate.performance: Acetate absorbs moderate moisture, well below viscose and cotton, and it is a comparatively weak fiber whose tenacity falls noticeably when wet, so abrasion and seam slippage limit it to low-stress uses such as linings. It is thermoplastic: a hot iron can glaze, shrink or fuse it. Acetone and acetone-based nail polish remover dissolve it. Because the esterified surface has few free hydroxyls, direct and reactive cotton dyes work poorly, and acetate is dyed with disperse dyes, a class developed specifically for it. Some disperse colors on acetate are prone to atmospheric fume fading.
acetate.identify: Burn tests are indicative only and should be done, if at all, on a tiny sample with safety precautions: acetate typically melts and burns, leaves a hard dark bead and gives an acrid, vinegar-like odor. The standard differential test is solubility, since acetate dissolves in acetone while triacetate and most other fibers do not. Microscopy shows lobed cross-sections. FTIR confirms ester carbonyl absorption. Acetate is frequently confused with viscose or silk in vintage garments.
acetate.labeling: In the United States, acetate is a generic name defined in 16 CFR 303.7 under the Textile Fiber Products Identification Act as a manufactured fiber whose fiber-forming substance is cellulose acetate; triacetate may be used where at least 92 percent of hydroxyl groups are acetylated. In the EU, Regulation (EU) No 1007/2011, Annex I, defines acetate as cellulose acetate fiber in which at least 74 but less than 92 percent of hydroxyl groups are acetylated. Trade names do not replace the generic name on a label.
acetate.past: The Swiss brothers Camille and Henri Dreyfus built a factory in England during the First World War to make cellulose diacetate dope, a coating used to tighten and protect the fabric skins of aircraft wings. When wartime demand ended they redirected the plant toward fiber, and in 1921 their company, British Celanese Ltd., began commercial production of diacetate yarn sold as Celanese. The new fiber would not take existing cotton dyes, and around 1923 British Celanese and the British Dyestuffs Corporation independently developed fine aqueous dispersions of sparingly soluble dyes, the origin of the disperse dye class later essential for polyester.
